text: A camera comes into the house as a lottery prize, which means nobody chose it and nobody can afford to keep it. Maria could sell it, and in a household counting coins against war and short wages that would be the sensible transaction; the film is about the years in which she does not make it. Jan Troell takes 131 minutes over this, and the length is the argument, since a life turns less on one decision than on the small permissions a woman is granted and then has taken back. What the camera does to her marriage matters as much as what it does to her eye. A craft picked up in the gaps between the work and the children. It took the Guldbagge for best film, and the pressure in it is not whether she can make pictures but what it costs her to go on making them.

The goal is a booking at the Rivoli, not a record deal, not a tour, one night on one stage. Two men have been chasing that long enough for the chase itself to become the act, and when the plan collapses it collapses sideways, into science fiction: Matt and Jay land in 2008. It is a well-chosen year to be stranded in, near enough to be misremembered rather than researched, far enough that the friendship they had then is not the one they have now. A hundred minutes run on the distance between what these two believe they are pulling off and what any room of strangers can plainly see. It took the Canadian Screen Award for best motion picture, an odd landing for a comedy about two people who have never once been given permission for anything.

Undercover work is a wage like any other, and this one has to cover a boy's upkeep and a sick wife's medicine. That arithmetic is the difference here: the fighting is not about honour or territory, it is about a household with no second income. Corey Yuen spends little of his 104 minutes making the gang interesting, because the pressure sits elsewhere — the man cannot resign, not this month, not while the medicine has to be bought. When another officer's carelessness breaks the cover, infiltration turns into escape, and the family is inside the problem rather than waiting at the edge of it. None of this stops it being an action picture. It only means every collision has a bill attached, and the film keeps counting the cost of a night's work in something other than bruises.

Pangaré is tired, which in a two-clown act is not a mood but a structural problem. His partner is his father, Puro Sangue, and the tent they own between them, the Circus Esperança, cannot spare either one for an evening. Selton Mello keeps the film to ninety minutes and stays mostly outside the ring, in the hours when a man paid to be funny is simply a man with a job and a family business. Nothing is diagnosed. Unhappiness here is an occupational condition, like a bad knee, and it raises the same practical question of who covers the work. Brazil put it forward as its submission to the Academy Awards, a considerable weight for a picture that never lifts its voice above the volume of a small circus in the afternoon.

Fanny arrives on a big black motorcycle, Zack behind her in leather and spikes, to take possession of a cottage in a Västergötland village that had other plans for it. Flogfält wanted to buy the place; the neighbours wanted the arrangement they already had; an unknown relative of the dead loner has made both impossible. Colin Nutley takes 127 minutes over a situation a sketch would settle in ten, and the surplus time is where the film lives, in how long a small community can stay courteous while working out what it will not put up with. The comedy is real. The property dispute underneath it is also real, and it decides who gets to stay. Everything turns on what a village believes it owns of the people who live in it.

In Patagonia the road does the work a plot usually does: it is long, it is the only one, and it puts unrelated people on the same line. Carlos Sorin sends three of them along it, and a baby, each carrying an errand that would sound like nothing if it were said out loud. The scale is deliberately mismatched, enormous country against minor purposes, and the humour comes from how seriously a person takes a small task when there is a full day of driving in which to rehearse it. Ninety-two minutes, and nobody in them is important. It took the Goya for best Ibero-American film, a large frame for three journeys a bus timetable could have contained. What the country supplies is time: enough of it that a small intention becomes a whole character.

There is not enough money for the dinner, and the dinner is not optional. Guests are coming, and the mother at the centre of Dariush Mehrjui's film has an afternoon to turn what is in the house into something that can be set in front of them. That is the whole engine of 108 minutes: hospitality as an obligation that does not consult the balance first. Comedy and pressure come from the same source, since every solution costs something the household cannot spare, and each is arrived at in complete seriousness. Mehrjui takes the meal as seriously as she does, which keeps the film from becoming a sketch about being poor. It took the Crystal Simorgh for best film. The suspense is whether a table can be made to tell a convincing story for one evening.

The most reasonable person in the ward is the one who says he is not from this planet. He is gentle, precise, and mainly critical of the way human beings treat each other, which is a hard argument to answer from inside an institution that has procedures for people who make it. His psychiatrist is not a happy man either, and has been instructed to proceed by the book. Eliseo Subiela lets the two of them sit against each other for 109 minutes without handing over a test that would settle where the patient came from, because that was never the interesting question. The science fiction consists of one calm claim, repeated, and it is enough to strain the ward's arrangements. It took the Silver Condor for best film. The plot is the order the doctor has been given: treat this man according to procedure, whatever he turns out to be.

An eight-year-old has appointed himself the repairman of a family that did not ask for one. Valentin lives with his grandmother in Buenos Aires at the end of the 1960s, and he moves through the adults' troubles with the confidence of someone who has not yet learned which of them are permanent. Alejandro Agresti holds it to eighty-three minutes, about the span of a child's account of anything. The film stays close to what the boy can gather, so the adults arrive in pieces and he does his arithmetic on incomplete numbers. Buenos Aires at that date is the address rather than the subject. What keeps the whole thing from turning sweet is that his plans are, in the way of eight-year-olds, entirely logical and aimed at the wrong problems.

The father turns seventy, so the daughters come home; that is the whole mechanism, and it is enough. Mia comes up from Stockholm. Her sisters, Eivor and Gunilla, are already there, having never left, and the three of them cannot get a conversation to arrive anywhere true. Each has built a life that requires the other two to have chosen wrongly. Maria Blom gives it ninety-eight minutes, most of them indoors, where the strain shows less in argument than in the pauses relatives leave for each other. A birthday is a hard deadline for people practised at avoidance: one house, one day, a celebration that has to be got through. It took the Guldbagge for best film. What it is good at is the particular carefulness of family members handling one another.

The source is a book written by the singer's mother, and that decides more about this film than casting could. Lucinha Araújo's Só as Mães São Felizes gives Walter Carvalho his vantage on a little over ten years of Cazuza's life, beginning in 1981 at the Circo Voador with Barão Vermelho and running into the solo career that followed. A rise that fast usually flattens into montage. What a mother's account supplies instead is the person who stayed still while it happened, and the house the noise came home to. Ninety-eight minutes for a decade of Brazilian rock, its venues and its speed. The film is less interested in explaining the songs than in registering what it costs a family when one of its members becomes public property.

Ninety-three minutes cut thirty-two ways leaves under three minutes a piece: too little to explain a man, about right for looking at one. François Girard declines the shape a life is usually given on film, in which the childhood accounts for the talent and the talent accounts for the solitude. What replaces it is a set of separate approaches to a Canadian pianist — his work, his character, the parts of a career that refuse to arrange themselves into a rise. The arithmetic is the argument. Portraiture by fragment leaves the joining to whoever is watching, and the gaps between the pieces carry as much as the pieces do. It is an odd way to write a biography and an exact way to describe a musician, whose real work was never conversation.

The marriage comes first, and what his family does reaches her afterward. Abdolhamid notices Faezeh at the market, they marry, and for a stretch the film is a courtship, which matters, because everything later depends on that marriage being credible rather than a device. Then the relatives in Sistan and Baluchestan enter it, along with what they do for a living, and Faezeh finds out how little standing a young wife has to object to the people her husband was born to. Narges Abyar builds 131 minutes around that lag: he has always had the whole map, and she is handed it a corner at a time. The pressure here is domestic long before it is criminal, and the first thing that cannot be left is a family.

A farce built on the life of Pablo Picasso, in which the facts turn up mainly to be tripped over. Tage Danielsson runs the painter from the early years to the late ones and treats the whole apparatus of the artist biography — the formative childhood, the famous encounters, the periods with names — as material for slapstick. A hundred and fifteen minutes is a long stretch to keep nonsense standing upright, and the length is part of the joke: the ceremonial shape of the great-man picture is maintained in full while nothing inside it behaves. Biography usually promises understanding. This one promises only that the years will be got through in order. It took the Guldbagge for best film, a peculiar landing for a comedy whose method is to refuse, at every opportunity, to be informative.
